scope: NY-7.NS.2a-3, NY-7.G.1 and the statistics/probability standards on the grade 7 test
notes: Resolved by lesson TITLE throughout. Grade 7 New York Unit 7 is Probability and Sampling and Unit 8 is Angles, Triangles, and Prisms (swapped relative to the national edition).

NY-7.SP.1 does not exist in the New York standards: CCSS 7.SP.1 and 7.SP.2 were moved down to NY-6.SP.1b and NY-6.SP.1c, and data/im_ms_reference.json maps no lesson to NY-7.SP.1 in either grade. Both items NYSED labels NY-7.SP.1 are box-plot reading (IQR; an outlier), which is NY-6.SP.4/5c content. The cluster heading NYSED prints for the code was ignored.

Imagine IM New York teaches ALL of the probability strand (NY-6.SP.6, 6.SP.7, 6.SP.8, 7.SP.8) in grade 7 Unit 7, even though New York numbers most of it as grade 6. So NY-6.SP.7 was searched and placed in grade 7.

g7-2026-026 has a defective published stem. The released PDF (2026 grade 7, PDF page 17) draws the expression as (4/5)(0.2)(-5/8); the transcription lost the parentheses around the third factor and prints it as a subtraction, which evaluates to -0.465 and matches no choice. The true value is -1/10, choice A. Placement follows the real expression.

g7-2024-040.quote: Evaluate the expressions in one of the columns.
g7-2024-040.why: The item evaluates a product of three signed factors, -2(-3)(4). The Row Game is the lesson's signed-multiplication practice set and is the only place students chain three signed factors, e.g. -10 * (3.2) * (-7.3).

g7-2025-023.why: The item asks for the product of -6 and -1 1/2: negative times negative, one factor a mixed number. Lesson 9 is where (neg)(neg) = pos is established, and its Cool-down tests exactly that with a decimal and a fraction factor.

g7-2026-015.why: The item multiplies -1/5 by 3/8 and asks for the signed fractional product. The Cool-down asks students to judge exactly that kind of computation, including a product of two signed fractions.

g7-2026-034.quote: A negative number divided by a negative number equals a
g7-2026-034.why: The item asks which expression is equivalent to (-45)/(-9) - i.e. that a negative divided by a negative is the corresponding positive quotient. This activity is where students state that rule in exactly those words.

g7-2026-004.quote: Match each expression with its value.
g7-2026-004.why: The item divides -5/6 by -1/3. Lesson 11 is the division-of-rational-numbers lesson and its Cool-down is where signed quotients are tested; note the curriculum never divides two negative FRACTIONS, so the reciprocal step comes from grade 6 Unit 4.

g7-2025-040.quote: evaluate the given expressions, and record your answers in the table
g7-2025-040.why: The item evaluates 0.5(4-6)/0.2, a numeric expression mixing decimals, a parenthesised difference and a fraction bar. This activity is the lesson's evaluate-expressions-with-rational-numbers task (including a ÷ -b); no IM activity does multi-step order of operations on a bare numeric expression.

g7-2026-047.quote: In this activity, students evaluate expressions using rational numbers.
g7-2026-047.why: The item evaluates (1/2)(-0.4) ÷ (1/3), mixing a fraction, a negative decimal and a division. This is the lesson where students evaluate expressions built from rational numbers with mixed forms and signs.

g7-2025-032.quote: A submarine is descending to examine the seafloor 2,100 feet below the surface.
g7-2025-032.why: The item has a submarine descending at a constant rate to a depth below sea level and asks for the depth after a longer time. The Cool-down of the negative-rates lesson poses the identical situation.

g7-2026-026.quote: This activity gives students an opportunity to practice multiplying signed numbers.
g7-2026-026.why: The real expression (see note) is (4/5)(0.2)(-5/8): a three-factor product mixing a fraction, a decimal and a negative fraction. The Row Game's columns are exactly that - e.g. (2.5) * (-3.25) and -4/3 * (-6/5).

g7-2023-008.quote: All 7 pencils have the same width. How wide is each pencil?
g7-2023-008.why: The item adds three mixed numbers and divides the total equally among 5 containers. Nothing in grade 7's rational-number unit does all-positive fraction arithmetic; this Cool-down is the two-step combine-then-share-equally task with mixed numbers.

g7-2023-040.quote: How many inches too high is the stack
g7-2023-040.why: The item multiplies 3/4 and 3/5 by 4 and asks how much farther one walker went. This activity is the curriculum's multi-step fraction word-problem set, including a 'how much more' difference of mixed numbers; no negatives are involved, so grade 7 Unit 5 does not ask it.

g7-2024-036.quote: Andre drank 1/2 of the water. How many liters of water did he drink?
g7-2024-036.why: The item takes 3/4 of 140 students and then 1/7 of that result - a fraction of a quantity, twice. This activity is where students decide that 'a fraction of a quantity' calls for multiplication and carry it out.

g7-2026-029.lessonTitle: Adding and Subtracting Decimals With Many Non-Zero Digits
g7-2026-029.quote: about addition and subtraction of numbers with more decimal places
g7-2026-029.why: The item chains four dollar amounts by 'more than' / 'less than' and subtracts the total from $800 - addition and subtraction of many-digit decimals only. That is this grade 6 lesson's business; grade 7 Unit 5's money work is all signed.

g7-2026-040.lessonTitle: Using Decimals in a Shopping Context
g7-2026-040.quote: Multiply and divide to find subtotal and total costs.
g7-2026-040.why: The item multiplies quantities (including 1/2 pound) by per-pound prices, totals them and finds the change from $20. This activity is the shopping-with-decimals task where students buy fractional pounds at listed prices and total the cost against a budget.

g7-2024-044.activity: Length of a Bus and Width of a Lake
g7-2024-044.quote: A scale drawing of a lake has a scale of 1 cm to 80 m.
g7-2024-044.why: The item runs actual -> drawing: given 1 cm = 50 mi and an actual 225 mi, find the map distance. Part 2 of this Cool-down is the same question in the same direction (actual lake width 1,000 m -> width on the drawing).

g7-2026-037.activity: Length of a Bus and Width of a Lake
g7-2026-037.quote: what is the width of the lake on the scale drawing?
g7-2026-037.why: Also actual -> drawing: given 1 in to 24 ft and an actual length of 76 4/5 ft, find the drawing length. Same Cool-down question, and the bus part shows the reverse direction for contrast.

g7-2023-045.quote: Find the actual area of the large rectangular pool. Show your reasoning.
g7-2023-045.why: The item reads a rectangular floor plan (1.5 in by 2 in at 1 in to 14 ft) and asks for the ACTUAL area in square feet. This is the only activity that asks for an actual area from a floor-plan scale drawing - and it is optional.

g7-2025-047.quote: Find the actual area of the large rectangular pool. Show your reasoning.
g7-2025-047.why: Same demand: an 8 in by 6 in sketch at 1 in to 1.75 ft, actual area in square feet. Drawing -> actual lengths -> area, which only this (optional) activity asks.

g7-2026-022.quote: Find the actual area of the large rectangular pool. Show your reasoning.
g7-2026-022.why: Same demand again, with the scale written backwards (1 ft to 1.5 cm), so students must divide rather than multiply before finding the actual area. Lesson 12 is also where scales are restated in equivalent forms.

g7-2024-014.quote: What measure of center is shown in the box plot? What measure of variability?
g7-2024-014.why: The item reads Q1 and Q3 off a single box plot and reports the IQR. This Cool-down asks literally for the measure of variability shown in a box plot and its value; IQR itself is first defined in grade 6 Unit 8 Lessons 15-16.

g7-2026-038.quote: Some histograms have a few data points that are unusually far from the center
g7-2026-038.why: The item asks what a point drawn apart from the box plot at 23 means - an outlier. This is the only student-facing place the idea 'unusually far from the rest' is named; IM never draws outliers outside a box plot's whiskers, so the display convention is not taught.

g7-2024-035.quote: Make dot plots to compare the heights of the tennis and badminton teams.
g7-2024-035.why: The item judges claims about the means and ranges of two dot-plotted groups. This is the lesson's compare-two-groups-from-dot-plots task; nothing in IM asks students to watch for two plots drawn on different scales, which is this item's real trap.

g7-2026-018.quote: How much taller is the volleyball team than the gymnastics team?
g7-2026-018.why: The item compares the average heights of two sets of 8 plants shown on dot plots with a common scale. This activity asks exactly that comparison of typical values between two groups.

g7-2025-035.quote: What is the difference between the sample medians for these two regions?
g7-2025-035.why: The item reads the medians of two box plots and subtracts them. This activity is the only place the curriculum asks for the numeric difference between two medians drawn from box plots.

g7-2023-016.quote: The IQR shown in box plot B is twice the IQR shown
g7-2023-016.why: The item judges four statements comparing the median, range, IQR and Q2 of two box plots. This Cool-down is the same exercise - agree/disagree with statements about the range, minimum and IQR of two box plots.

g7-2026-014.quote: Sort the data from least to greatest, and then find the median.
g7-2026-014.why: The item finds and compares medians, one from a frequency table of 17 values and one from a dot plot. This is the lesson that introduces finding the median from ordered data and from a dot plot; IM never reads a median off a frequency table, which is why this item is hard.

g7-2023-034.lessonTitle: Keeping Track of All Possible Outcomes
g7-2023-034.quote: what is the probability it will be a necklace that fits Andre’s requirements?
g7-2023-034.why: The item counts the 2x2x3 sandwich combinations and gives the probability of one particular combination. This activity counts a multi-attribute sample space and then asks for the probability of one specified combination.

g7-2024-047.lessonTitle: Keeping Track of All Possible Outcomes
g7-2024-047.quote: How many different necklaces are possible? Explain your reasoning.
g7-2024-047.why: The item counts 3x3x2 = 18 movie/snack/drink combinations and reports the probability of one of them as a fraction. Same activity, same three-attribute counting-then-probability move.

g7-2025-041.quote: Suppose you roll two number cubes. What is the probability of getting:
g7-2025-041.why: The item spins two spinners and asks for the probability that the PRODUCT is odd - an event defined by a relation between both results. This activity asks the same kind of question of two number cubes (same number, exactly one even, sum of 8).

g7-2023-044.lessonTitle: Keeping Track of All Possible Outcomes
g7-2023-044.quote: Consider the experiment: Flip a coin, and then roll a number cube.
g7-2023-044.why: The item is that experiment verbatim - flip a fair coin and roll a number cube - and asks for the number of outcomes plus the sample space. This activity builds that sample space three ways.

g7-2025-003.lessonTitle: Keeping Track of All Possible Outcomes
g7-2025-003.quote: Priya draws a tree with branches in which each pathway represents a different outcome
g7-2025-003.why: The item asks which tree diagram represents 3 main courses x 2 desserts. This activity is where the tree representation of a sample space is introduced and compared with lists and tables.

g7-2026-008.lessonTitle: Keeping Track of All Possible Outcomes
g7-2026-008.quote: How many different shirts are available with these options?
g7-2026-008.why: The item counts 4 foods x 3 juices = 12 combinations, with no probability asked. The Cool-down asks for the count of combinations from listed options in exactly that form.

g7-2024-007.quote: Sort the histograms into 2 groups based on whether they are approximately symmetrical or not.
g7-2024-007.why: The item picks the true statement about a dot plot's distribution from options naming symmetry, range, an outlier and a cluster. This activity is where that whole vocabulary - symmetric, peaks, gaps, values unusually far from the center - is taught.

g7-2023-031.quote: How many students responded to the questions?
g7-2023-031.why: The item counts the observations on a dot plot (27 players). This Cool-down asks the identical question of a dot plot and is tagged to the reporting-the-number-of-observations standard.

g7-2025-039.quote: How many dogs weigh at least 120 pounds?
g7-2025-039.why: The item sums a histogram's bars to get the number of students surveyed. This activity is where students read and add frequencies off histogram bars; no IM activity asks for the total number of observations in a histogram outright.

g7-2026-030.quote: Determine if each of these would be an appropriate label to represent the data
g7-2026-030.why: The item picks which label (number of cats / years / inches / pounds) correctly names the attribute and unit on a dot plot's number line. This Warm-up offers the same menu of candidate labels and asks students to include the unit of measurement.

g7-2023-009.quote: Find the modes for these data sets.
g7-2023-009.why: The item finds the mode of ten scores and compares it to the median. Lesson 9 (a New York addition) is the only place the mode is defined and found; the median arrives later in Lesson 13, and no lesson compares the two.

g7-2026-045.quote: Estimate the number of DVDs that will be checked out for every 100 patrons.
g7-2026-045.why: The item takes a frequency table for 32 students and predicts the chocolate count among 120. This Cool-down does the same thing with a frequency table of 10 patrons scaled to 100, and the lesson is the one that addresses NY-6.SP.7.
